title: India detains thousands as 'Cockroach' youth movement protests voter list revision
summary: Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide…

image.caption: Protesters are detained by security personnel during a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which is seeking the resignation of India's chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, near the protest site in New Delhi on Saturday. (Adnan Abidi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Election Commission, government reject allegations of voter manipulation
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 10, 2026 10:10 AM EDT | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago

Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India’s capital, chasing off some and detaining many others.

Some demonstrators were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centres. Several leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with opposition lawmakers and student activists, were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.

The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes.
Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.

blocks.text: Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi’s party, dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchic elements."
"Their flop show has been completely demolished," Patra said.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.
The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July.
Security tight around protest site

Movement leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, but were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the party on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas, with police briefly detaining some of them.
Protesters shout from a police bus after being detained in New Delhi on Saturday. (Adnan Abidi/Reuters)
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn’t we fight for our rights?" said Tanya Negi, a college student who travelled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?"

The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi’s government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world’s largest democracy.
The latest crackdown renewed criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police.
Voter list dispute raises election concerns

The protests centre on India’s Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner, and an end to the change, which has so far removed more than 130 million names from voter lists.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
Police officers detain a protester during a Saturday demonstration in New Delhi. (Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday’s planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
Youth movement targets Modi
For the CJP movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
Police prevent a detained protester from trying to escape from a bus during a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi on Saturday (Adnan Abidi/Reuters)

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge almost midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear.
National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.
